name: Tara Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader underground at the Marrow Creek copper mine. It's what we call an LHD, a load-haul-dump machine, basically a long, low front-end loader that mucks out the broken rock after a blast and tips it down the ore pass. Shift starts with the bus down the decline, then a toolbox talk, then it's you, the headlights and about four hundred metres of rock overhead. I like the rhythm of it and the women's change room is a good laugh, but the dust and the noise get into your bones by the end of the week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what does life look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mike is a porter at the district hospital, so between us we're not on big money, and I'm on the lower end of the loader rates because I never pushed for the top tickets. Our two boys have left home, and we lent the youngest his rental bond last year, so savings are about three weeks of bills, if that. I'm fifty-eight, and the plan is to work to sixty-two and then do something gentler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, all that worry for a better spell-checker. I'd probably share some joke about it in the family group chat. At work we'd have a laugh about the managers who bought the fancy software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved but not surprised. Underground, the change was always going to be slow, because the rock doesn't care how clever your computer is. My job would look much the same until I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just carry on, keep my head down and try to put a bit more away for when I stop. Maybe I'd use the chatbot on my phone now and then like I do already, to check a pension letter or write an email to the council. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit flat, like when a storm warning comes to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you already use a chatbot sometimes. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I asked it to explain my pension statement, because the fund writes like it's trying to hide something. It was decent, though I still rang the union rep to check it. I trust it about as much as I trust the shift boss's weather forecast: worth hearing, not worth betting on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about work that would worry you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The remote-control loaders. They've been trialling one where a man sits on the surface in a chair with screens and drives it. That's not really AI, it's more like a video game, and it's coming either way, but slowly.

S0.say: I'd tell people it was a lot of worry over a better spell-checker. I'd joke about it in the family group chat and laugh at work about the managers who bought the fancy software.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved but not surprised, because change underground was always going to be slow. I think my job would look much the same until I retire.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and tries to put a little more aside before retiring at sixty-two. Keeps using a chatbot now and then to check pension letters or write emails.
S0.feel: Calm, a little flat, like a storm warning that came to nothing.
S0.quote: I trust it about as much as I trust the shift boss's weather forecast: worth hearing, not worth betting on.
S0.fieldNote: Tara is practical and dry, and already uses a chatbot in a limited, checking way. In this picture the slow remote-control loader trial is the only cloud. Her line about trusting AI like the shift boss's forecast sums up her steady approach: try it, but verify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need a seat at the table when they bring in the new kit, not a memo after it's done. I'd be pushing our union for training paid on company time, especially for the women and the older crews who always get left to last. I'd post the union's statement, that's about as far as I go online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think the remote loaders would speed up, and then the automated ones that run on their own down the drives. I'm average at this job, not a star, so I wouldn't be first in line for the good seats on the surface. Four years to sixty-two suddenly looks like a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for the remote-operator training as soon as they offered it, even if it meant day shifts in a room with no windows. We'd cut back on eating out and I'd sell the caravan we never use, that'd give us maybe four thousand to sit on. And I'd ask Mike to look at whether the hospital needs anyone in stores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can handle. It's pressure I can see, and that's better than pressure I can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sit in a room with screens instead of going underground. How would that feel, after all these years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange. I'd miss the bus ride down and the smell, believe it or not. I've spent thirty years wishing I was out of the dust, and now I'd be fighting to keep my seat in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dot, who runs the water cart, she's sixty and hates computers more than anything. And the young guys who just got their loader tickets, because they've got mortgages and no fallback. They'd need the union more than me.

S1.say: I'd say workers need a seat at the table when the new equipment comes in, not a memo afterwards. I'd push the union for paid training, especially for women and older crews who get left until last.
S1.think: Off the record, I'd expect remote and automated loaders to come faster, and as an average operator I wouldn't be first in line for the surface seats. Four years to sixty-two would suddenly feel long.
S1.do: Volunteers for remote-operator training as soon as it's offered and sells the unused caravan for about four thousand. Cuts back on eating out and asks her partner to look into stores jobs at the hospital.
S1.feel: Anxious but in control, because she can see the pressure coming.
S1.quote: I've spent thirty years wishing I was out of the dust, and now I'd be fighting to keep my seat in it.
S1.fieldNote: Tara's steady side shows: she won't lead the change but she'll step forward once a proven option exists, like the remote-operator room. Her union politics focus on fairness for women and older crews. The irony of fighting to stay in the dust she always wanted to leave was the best moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs government stepping in, fast. A pause on mass layoffs, income support for people who lose work, and a tax on the companies doing the replacing. I'd be at the rally if the union called one, and I'd bring Mike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, in two years they wouldn't need me or the man in the remote chair. I'd be sixty with three weeks of savings. The machine I drive would just drive itself, and I'd be the one standing at the top of the decline with my lunchbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the union to find out the redundancy terms and I'd take the payout if it was decent rather than wait to be pushed. We'd sell the caravan and the second car. I'd ask the pension fund about early access and I'd look for anything with people, aged care or the hospital, because a robot can't hold someone's hand. Or maybe it can by then, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry underneath it. Like the floor went out from under me just before the finish line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning let you do, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much more than brace. Two years doesn't get me to sixty-two, and there'd be no time for a new trade to pay off. I'd spend it saving every cent and hoping the government moves faster than it usually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your boys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to lend us money, we'd sort it, and then I'd probably need to borrow some. The eldest has a baby, so he's got his own worries. I'd tell them to get into something where you have to be in the room with people.

S2.say: I'd say the government needs to step in fast with a pause on mass layoffs, income support and a tax on the companies doing the replacing. I'd go to a union rally and bring my partner.
S2.think: Privately, in two years they wouldn't need me or even the remote operator, and I'd be sixty with three weeks' savings. I'd be the one standing at the top of the decline with a lunchbox and nowhere to go.
S2.do: Checks redundancy terms with the union straight away and takes a decent payout rather than waiting to be pushed. Sells the caravan and second car, asks about early pension access, and looks for work in aged care or the hospital.
S2.feel: Frightened, with anger underneath, as if the floor went out just before the finish line.
S2.quote: The machine I drive would just drive itself, and I'd be the one standing at the top of the decline with my lunchbox.
S2.fieldNote: Two years shuts every door Tara was relying on, including the remote-operator room. She moves quickly and practically, taking the payout and looking at care work, but admits she can't be sure even that is safe. She wants strong government action and sees this as a political fight, not just a personal one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for a proper transition plan, mine by mine, with the union in the room. I'd want the company to fund retraining and a bridge to pension for anyone over fifty-five. That's what I'd say at meetings and in the comments on the union page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three, and that's past my target. If I can hang on, I'd squeak through. The worry is the last two years, when they're running down the crews and nobody knows who goes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the remote-operator course early, in the first year, so I'm useful during the changeover. I'd sell the caravan now rather than later and put the money in the bank. And I'd start doing a few shifts a month at the hospital kitchen with Mike's help, so I've got a foot somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a bit of hope in it. Like running for the bus and seeing the driver wait for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So compared with the two-year picture, what's the biggest difference for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to be useful on the way down. With two years I'm just in the way. With five years, I'm the woman who knows the drives and can tell the robot where the bad ground is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pick up work at the hospital kitchen. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. Mike says they're always short on weekends, and I've done kitchens before the mine. It's a quarter of the pay, but it's a door.

S3.say: I'd say this is when we need a proper transition plan, mine by mine, with the union in the room. The company should fund retraining and a bridge to pension for anyone over fifty-five.
S3.think: Privately, five years gets me past sixty-two, so if I can hang on I'd just about make it. What worries me is the last couple of years, when crews get run down and nobody knows who goes next.
S3.do: Takes the remote-operator course in the first year to stay useful during the changeover and sells the caravan early to bank the money. Starts a few weekend shifts in the hospital kitchen as a backup.
S3.feel: Anxious with some hope in it, like seeing the bus driver wait for her.
S3.quote: With five years, I'm the woman who knows the drives and can tell the robot where the bad ground is.
S3.fieldNote: Five years flips Tara from bracing to planning: she sees herself as useful during the changeover because she knows the ground. She builds a small second income in a kitchen, a practical hedge rather than a dream. Her union politics stay constant across all the AGI pictures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so let's not waste it like we wasted the warnings about the smelter closing. Proper apprenticeships for whatever comes next, and the company paying into a fund for the town. That's what I'd want the union to fight for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, so I'm out before it hits me. My worry is the boys and the grandbaby, and whether there's a town left for them. For me, honestly, it's mostly about getting to sixty-two in one piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and try to put a hundred a fortnight away, which is more than we manage now. I'd nag the eldest about getting a trade in something like solar or care. And I'd keep using the chatbot here and there, because if I'm going to be the old lady who understands this stuff a bit, I might as well start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a worry in the back for the kids. Like a nagging tooth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the smelter. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They announced it would close in eight years and everyone just carried on, me included. Then it shut and suddenly everyone was surprised. Eight years and nobody retrained, nobody saved, because it always felt far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would you do differently this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make the boys sit down and actually talk about it at Christmas, not just say it'll be fine. I'm not scared of the robots in 2036, I'm scared of us all saying we've got plenty of time.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a chance we shouldn't waste like we wasted the warnings about the smelter. We need real apprenticeships for what's next and the company paying into a fund for the town.
S4.think: Off the record, by 2036 I'm sixty-eight and out of it, so for me it's about reaching sixty-two in one piece. My real worry is my sons, the grandbaby and whether the town survives.
S4.do: Keeps working and tries to save a hundred a fortnight. Pushes her eldest son towards a trade in solar or care, and keeps using a chatbot now and then to stay familiar with the tools.
S4.feel: Mostly settled, with a nagging worry about her children in the background.
S4.quote: I'm not scared of the robots in 2036, I'm scared of us all saying we've got plenty of time.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Tara's own path is clear, so her focus moves to her sons and the town. The smelter story is her proof that long warnings get wasted, and it shapes her plan to force a family conversation. She sees a small edge in being the older person who understands the tools a bit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything else gives me time to get to sixty-two, that one doesn't. What would help is the government guaranteeing an income bridge for older workers, and the union making sure women aren't the first ones pushed out. Give me a fair way out and I'll take it with a smile, just don't make me beg for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the women. There aren't many of us underground and we fought to get there. It'd be a bitter thing if the robots were the ones that finally pushed us back out.

headlineQuote: Give me a fair way out and I'll take it with a smile, just don't make me beg for it.
portrait: Tara Schmidt is 58 and runs an underground loader at the Marrow Creek copper mine, a long, low machine that clears blasted rock. She and her partner Mike, a hospital porter, have about three weeks of savings after lending their son his rental bond, and she aims to retire at sixty-two. She's a steady, practical union member who uses a chatbot now and then but always checks it. She moves from calm in the hype picture to alarmed when AGI comes in two years, then plans her way through the slower versions with retraining, a kitchen job on the side and pushes for her sons to find work with people. She wants a fair, dignified way out, especially for women in the mine.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it's the only one that ends her work before she can reach sixty-two.
whatWouldHelp: A government-guaranteed income bridge for older workers, and the union making sure women aren't pushed out first.
